stem: A 70-year-old man is scheduled for bilateral knee replacement. During the preoperative verification, the surgical team notes the wrong knee is listed for surgery. The patient confirms it is the opposite knee, and the surgical site has not been marked yet. What is the most appropriate next step?

opts.t: Perform a preoperative “time-out” and verification with the surgical team and patient before marking the correct site
Proceed and check later in the operating room
Cancel the surgery and reschedule without further verification

expl: Wrong-site surgery is prevented by verification with the patient and team (time-out) and correct site marking before surgery.

why.B: Leaving verification to the OR invites a wrong-site error.
why.C: Cancelling is unnecessary; the error can be corrected by verification.
why.D: Site decisions are never left to intra-operative judgement.

stem: A patient admitted for elective surgery suddenly develops shock and becomes confused, requiring emergency surgical intervention. There is no available family member or contact to provide consent. What is the most appropriate course of action?

opts.t: Continue trying to find a family member
Perform the surgery immediately because it is an emergency
Delay surgery until consent is obtained

expl: Life-threatening emergency, patient lacks capacity, no surrogate available → implied consent; operate immediately.

why.A: Cancelling would let the patient die.
why.B: Searching for family delays life-saving surgery.
why.D: Waiting for consent in shock is unsafe.

stem: a long emergency case what should you do regarding the surgery consent?

opts.t: Hold OR and wait for spouse consent
2 surgeons call the spouse and sign in behalf of her
No need for consent because it’s an emergency

expl: In a true emergency where the patient can't consent and no one is available, implied consent applies.

why.A: Holding a life-saving operation is wrong.
why.C: A fingerprint from an incapacitated patient is not valid consent.

stem: 50yp Patient admitted to do hemicolectomy, you attended the procedure from the beginning to the end. You noticed the nurse saying “All instruments, and sponges are out” From which interval of the safety checklist is this sentence from?

opts.t: It is not important to say it

expl: "All instruments and sponges are out" = the counts confirmed in the SIGN OUT, before the patient leaves the OR.

why.B: Sign in is before induction (identity, site, consent).
why.C: Time out is before incision (team, critical events, antibiotics).
why.D: Counts are essential to prevent retained items.

stem: The meaning of a near miss event ?

opts.t: An adverse event that harms the patient
incident which could have caused unacceptable consequences but did not occur
an incident which occurs but did not harm the patients

expl: A near miss could have caused harm/unacceptable consequences but did not, thanks to chance or timely interception.

why.C: An incident that reached the patient without harm is a "no-harm incident", not a near miss (a near miss doesn't reach/harm the patient).

stem: A patient presented with a life-threatening vascular injury after a RTA. No watcher was there in the scene. What to do regarding his consent?

opts.t: Try to find a family member
Try to get a verbal consent from a family member

expl: Life-threatening injury and no one available → implied consent; treat immediately.

stem: In general precautions, which of the following should be avoided?

opts.t: Sharp instruments discarded in special sharp container
Drapes should be placed in containers
Needles should be resheathed by the same person
Gloves and gown should be removed after all used equipment

srcNote: (Patient safety) (practical procedures & investigations of surgical patients)
expl: Re-sheathing (re-capping) needles is the classic cause of needle-stick injury and must be avoided; sharps go straight into a sharps container.

why.A: This is correct practice, not something to avoid.

stem: A 55-year-old male is planned for hernia repair. He is comprehensive with no mental illness. During the preoperative assessment visit, he didn't come to the clinic and his 20-year-old son came to sign the consent on his behalf. What is the most appropriate action?

opts.t: Ask for the older brother to sign the consent
Ask for the patient himself to sign the consent
Get the medical director approval for the son to sign the consent
Let the son sign the consent

expl: A competent adult must sign his own consent; relatives can't consent for a patient who has capacity.

why.C: Not needed — the patient can sign.
why.D: The son can't consent for a competent father.

stem: Which of the following is considered a human factor in patient safety?
expl: Human factors are errors made by the people involved (knowledge, judgement, fatigue) — e.g. misusing/misinterpreting investigations. Staffing levels are an organizational factor, similar drugs a medication factor, and new technology a technological factor.

opts.t: marking the site of the patient

srcNote: Both A and B are correct (Pre-operative assessment)
expl: The WHO "sign in" (before induction) confirms the patient's identity, the site, procedure and consent, and checks that the site is marked. The source listed both A and B as correct; confirming identity (B) is the core step — the marking itself is done earlier and only checked here. "Anticipating critical events" and team introductions belong to the time-out.

why.A: Accepted by the source too — sign-in checks that the site has been marked.
why.B: Correct — confirming identity is the core of sign-in.

stem: what is done in sign out?
expl: In the sign out, the nurse verbally confirms the name of the procedure performed, the counts, specimen labelling and equipment problems.

why.B: Identity is confirmed in sign in.
why.C: Consent is checked in sign in.
why.D: Expected blood loss is discussed in sign in/time out.

stem: which of the following represents human factor that results in adverse event in patient care?
expl: Human factors are errors made by the people giving care — e.g. an error in doing an investigation. Similar drug names are a medication/system factor, new technology is a technological factor and staffing levels are an organizational factor.

stem: While you're in 453 surg course, you attended laparoscopic appendectomy and the surgeon complained that there is no gas. The nurse went to bring another gas tank, your fellow intern told you to connect the oxygen tank. What would tell him?

opts.t: Sorry I will use anesthesia nitrous oxide instead
Sorry I will use room air instead

srcNote: (Principles of laparoscopic surgery) gas traits: not inflammable like oxygen’ Dr notes
expl: Laparoscopy needs a non-flammable, highly soluble gas — CO₂. Oxygen supports combustion (diathermy fire) and can embolize; nitrous oxide supports combustion and room air risks fatal air embolism.

why.C: N₂O supports combustion — unsafe with diathermy.
why.D: Room air (nitrogen) is poorly soluble → gas embolism.

stem: Which one of the following should be included in the informed consent?
srcNote: (Patient safety) Informed consent: Details & accuracy of the dx, the goal and details of the planned procedure, complications, prognosis, other tx options, advantages and possibility of success, name of responsible surgeon, at any time, the patient can change his or her mind.
expl: Informed consent includes the diagnosis, the planned procedure, complications, prognosis, other options, and the name of the responsible surgeon.

stem: “Sign in” involves which of the following?
srcNote: (Patient safety) Sign in: Confirmation of patient identity Site and nature of procedure Obtaining consent Marking the site of procedure
expl: Sign in = confirm patient identity, site, procedure, consent, site marking (before induction). Counting gauzes = sign out.

stem: Patient died due to medication interaction , as a health care provider what first action will you do?

opts.t: Omit further use of the intended drug.

expl: After a sentinel event (death from a drug interaction) the first step is a root cause analysis — a systematic look for the underlying system causes, without blame.

why.A: Punishment discourages reporting and doesn't fix the system.
why.C: FMEA is proactive — used before an event to find possible failures.
why.D: Premature; the cause is not yet known.

stem: Which one of the following in hazard classification deal with radiation; laser, furniture, floors,building, storage?
expl: Source key B. Radiation, laser, furniture, floors, buildings and storage are hazards of the physical environment ("physical hazards"); this version prints "physiological". Ergonomic hazards relate to posture/lifting; environmental hazards to air, water and waste.

why.A: Environmental hazards are air, water, waste, chemicals.
why.B: Correct (source key — read as physical hazard).
why.C: Codes for fire, disaster and evacuation.

stem: Which one of the following in hazard classification deal with radiation, laser, furniture, floors, buildings, storage?
expl: Radiation, laser, furniture, floors, buildings and storage are physical hazards.
